lessons.title: Math is Playful
lessons.objective: I can use patterns and relationships to make sense of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle and think logically about its solutions.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe a puzzle strategy using the words pattern, rule, and predict.

concept.heading: Playing with math means playing with patterns
concept.intro: The objective is to move the whole stack of discs to another rod. The rules: move only one disc at a time, move only the top disc from a stack, and never place a larger disc on top of a smaller disc.
concept.keyIdea: Algorithmic Thinking & Recursive Patterns. 1. Deconstruct complex multi-step problems into smaller, repeatable sub-tasks. 2. Trace patterns from simple cases to formulate general mathematical rules. 3. Verify algorithmic rules across edge cases and increasing problem sizes

worked.title: Watch me imagine the solution first
lines: Before moving anything, I describe what the solved puzzle will look like: the discs in the same order — smallest on top to largest on bottom — but on a different rod.
Then I play the small cases: a one-disc tower takes 1 move, and a two-disc tower takes 3 moves.
A three-disc tower takes at least 7 moves. Small cases are how mathematicians play.
linesEs: Antes de mover nada, describo cómo se verá el rompecabezas resuelto: los discos en el mismo orden — el más pequeño arriba y el más grande abajo — pero en otra varilla.
Luego juego los casos pequeños: una torre de un disco toma 1 movimiento, y una de dos discos toma 3 movimientos.
Una torre de tres discos toma al menos 7 movimientos. Los casos pequeños son la forma en que juegan los matemáticos.

together.title: Let's organize the moves in a table
lines: Discs: 1, 2, 3 — Steps: 1, 3, 7. What is happening from each row to the next?
Double the number of steps and add 1: 1 doubled plus 1 is 3, and 3 doubled plus 1 is 7.
So 4 discs take 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps, and 5 discs take 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps.
The pattern just solved a puzzle we never touched.
linesEs: Discos: 1, 2, 3 — Pasos: 1, 3, 7. ¿Qué pasa de una fila a la siguiente?
Duplica el número de pasos y suma 1: 1 duplicado más 1 es 3, y 3 duplicado más 1 es 7.
Entonces 4 discos toman 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 pasos, y 5 discos toman 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 pasos.
El patrón acaba de resolver un rompecabezas que nunca tocamos.
together.titleEs: Organicemos los movimientos en una tabla

vocabulary.definition: A problem designed to be played with — it has rules, a goal, and room to imagine solutions.
vocabulary.example: Tower of Hanoi: three rods, a stack of discs, and two rules.

vocabulary.definition: Something that repeats or changes in a predictable way.
vocabulary.example: Circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle …

vocabulary.definition: A rule that tells you how to get the next value in a pattern from the one before it.
vocabulary.example: 1 → 3 → 7 → 15: the rule is “double it and add 1”.

vocabulary.definition: To say what will happen before it happens, using a pattern or reasoning.
vocabulary.example: We counted towers of 1, 2 and 3 discs. Reach PAST them: the rule says 5 discs takes 31 steps — before moving one.

vocabulary.definition: To arrange information — often in a table — so patterns become easier to see.
vocabulary.example: Discs 1, 2, 3 in one column and steps 1, 3, 7 in the next.

lessons.title: Math is Ingenuity
lessons.objective: I can use ratios and models to explain how the Penny Farthing and gear-driven bicycles were ingenious solutions to a real problem.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain a gear ratio using the words rotation, teeth, and 'for each ___, the wheel turns ___.'

concept.heading: Math can power ingenious solutions
concept.intro: The Penny Farthing is powered by the rider: pushing the pedals rotates the front wheel directly, so each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time — a 1 to 1 ratio.
concept.keyIdea: Gear Ratios, Circumference & Mechanical Advantage. Formula: Distance = Rotations × Circumference | Gear Ratio = Teeth_Driver / Teeth_Driven. 1. Circumference is the distance traveled in one full wheel rotation. 2. Gear ratios determine speed and rotational force (torque). 3. Apply proportional reasoning to calculate travel distance and mechanical advantage

worked.title: Watch me use a gear ratio
lines: A later bicycle design uses a chain: the pedal gear has 48 teeth, and the largest rear gear has 32 teeth.
For each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear, the wheel gear also turns 48 teeth.
The 32-tooth gear needs to turn 32 teeth to make one full rotation, so I find the equivalent ratio: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5.
The rear wheel makes 1.5 rotations for each pedal rotation — this gear makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds or go uphill.
linesEs: Un diseño posterior de bicicleta usa una cadena: el engranaje del pedal tiene 48 dientes, y el engranaje trasero más grande tiene 32 dientes.
Por cada vuelta del engranaje de 48 dientes, el engranaje de la rueda también recorre 48 dientes.
El engranaje de 32 dientes necesita recorrer 32 dientes para dar una vuelta completa, así que hallo la razón equivalente: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5.
La rueda trasera da 1.5 vueltas por cada vuelta de pedal — este engranaje hace más fácil pedalear despacio o subir una cuesta.
worked.titleEs: Mírame usar una razón de engranaje

together.title: Let's do the smallest gear together
lines: The smallest rear gear has 12 teeth, and the pedal gear still turns 48 teeth per rotation.
One full rotation of the 12-tooth gear takes 12 teeth.
48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the rear wheel makes 4 rotations for each pedal rotation.
This gear makes it easier to pedal at faster speeds or go downhill.
linesEs: El engranaje trasero más pequeño tiene 12 dientes, y el engranaje del pedal sigue recorriendo 48 dientes por vuelta.
Una vuelta completa del engranaje de 12 dientes toma 12 dientes.
48 ÷ 12 = 4, así que la rueda trasera da 4 vueltas por cada vuelta de pedal.
Este engranaje hace más fácil pedalear rápido o bajar una cuesta.
together.titleEs: Hagamos juntos el engranaje más pequeño

vocabulary.definition: Coming up with different, and sometimes unique, solutions to problems.
vocabulary.example: The Penny Farthing's huge wheel, then chains and gears — two clever fixes.

vocabulary.definition: One full turn of a wheel, gear, or pedal all the way around.
vocabulary.example: One full turn of the pedal — 360° all the way around.

vocabulary.definition: A toothed wheel that passes motion to another toothed wheel through a chain.
vocabulary.example: A 48-tooth pedal gear pulling a 12-tooth wheel gear through the chain.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two quantities, like pedal rotations to wheel rotations.
vocabulary.example: 48 pedal teeth to 12 wheel teeth — 4 wheel turns for every pedal turn.

vocabulary.definition: Ratios that make the same comparison using different numbers.
vocabulary.example: 1 : 4 and 3 : 12 describe the same gear, at different sizes.

Predict before checking a new design.
Explain how a useful constraint can lead to more creative solutions.

support.prompt: What is the fewest number of moves needed to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
support.explanation: It takes at least 7 moves to solve a three-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle.
feedback: 3 is the number of DISCS — moving each disc only once is impossible because of the size rule.
6 doubles the 3 discs but forgets the extra move — the pattern is double and add 1, so 3 discs need 7.
9 is 3 × 3, but the fewest-moves count follows the doubling pattern, not disc × disc.
hints: It is more than one move per disc.
A two-disc tower already takes 3 moves.
Double 3 and add 1.

support.prompt: Which move is against the rules of the Tower of Hanoi?
choices: Moving one disc at a time
Moving the top disc from a stack
Placing a larger disc on top of a smaller disc
Placing a smaller disc on top of a larger disc
support.explanation: A larger disc can never be on top of a smaller disc — that is the rule that makes the puzzle a puzzle.
feedback: One disc at a time is exactly what the rules require, not what they forbid.
You may only move the TOP disc of a stack — that move follows the rules.
Smaller on top of larger is the legal direction; it is the reverse that is banned.
hints: Two of these are the rules themselves.
Think about disc SIZES.
Which stacking order would crush a smaller disc?

support.prompt: What will the solved puzzle look like?
choices: The discs in the same order — smallest on top to largest on bottom — but on a different rod
The discs in reverse order, largest on top
The discs spread out with one disc on each rod
The discs back on the starting rod in any order
support.explanation: The goal is to rebuild the whole stack, smallest to largest, on a different rod.
feedback: Largest on top would break the rule — a larger disc can never sit on a smaller one.
Spreading the discs out is a middle step, not the finished puzzle.
The stack must END on a different rod, and the size order is required, not optional.
hints: Imagine the ending before you start.
The stack looks just like the start.
Only its rod has changed.

support.prompt: How many moves does a one-disc tower take? A two-disc tower?
support.explanation: You can solve a one-disc tower in 1 step and a two-disc tower in 3 steps.
feedback: 2 moves is not enough for two discs — the small disc must move aside, the large disc moves, then the small disc moves back on top: 3 moves.
4 moves is one too many for two discs — the fewest is 3.
One disc needs only 1 move — just lift it to another rod.
hints: Play the one-disc game in your head first.
For two discs: the small one has to get out of the way, and later get back on top.
Count those three separate moves.

support.prompt: The number of discs in a Tower of Hanoi puzzle can vary. What NEVER varies?
support.explanation: The number of rods never varies — there are always three rods, no matter how many discs the puzzle uses.

support.prompt: On the Penny Farthing, what is the ratio of pedal rotations to front-wheel rotations?
support.explanation: The pedals are attached directly to the front wheel, so each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time — a 1 to 1 ratio.
feedback: 1 to 2 would mean each pedal rotation turns the wheel twice, but the pedals are attached directly to the wheel.
1 to 4 describes the chain bike's smallest gear, not the Penny Farthing.
2 to 1 would mean the rider must pedal twice for one wheel turn, but one pedal rotation gives one wheel rotation.
hints: The pedals are attached directly to the front wheel.
One pedal rotation makes the wheel turn how many times?
Each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time.

support.prompt: How far does the Penny Farthing travel with each pedal rotation?
choices: The length of the perimeter of the front wheel
It does not move a fixed distance
support.explanation: One wheel rotation rolls the bike forward exactly the perimeter of the wheel, and one pedal rotation makes one wheel rotation.
feedback: The rider's height does not determine rolling distance — the wheel's perimeter does.
The pedal's length changes how hard you have to push, not how far the wheel rolls in one turn.
It does move a fixed distance — one full roll of the wheel is always the same length.
hints: Picture the wheel rolling one full turn on the ground.
The distance it covers is the distance all the way around the wheel.
That distance around the wheel is its perimeter.

support.prompt: Why was the front wheel of the Penny Farthing so large?
choices: So the bicycle is easier to stop
So the rider sits closer to the ground
So the bicycle travels a greater distance with one pedal rotation
So the rear wheel spins faster
support.explanation: A bigger wheel has a longer perimeter, so each pedal rotation carries the rider farther.
feedback: A huge front wheel actually made the Penny Farthing harder, not easier, to stop.
The large wheel puts the rider high UP, not close to the ground.
The rear wheel is not pedaled at all — the front wheel does the work.
hints: Each pedal rotation moves the bike one perimeter of the wheel.
Compare the perimeter of a big wheel and a small wheel.
A bigger wheel means a longer distance per pedal rotation.

support.prompt: For each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear, how many teeth does the wheel gear turn?
support.explanation: The chain links the gears, so one full rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear pulls 48 teeth of chain past the wheel gear.
feedback: One rotation moves every tooth on the pedal gear past the chain, not just one.
12 is the tooth count of the smallest rear gear, not the number of teeth the chain moves.
32 is the tooth count of the largest rear gear, not the number of teeth the chain moves.
hints: The chain moves one link for each tooth on the pedal gear.
Read the tooth count printed on the pedal gear in the question.
Count the teeth the chain pulls in one full turn of the pedal gear — that is how many the wheel gear turns.

support.prompt: How does the size of the front wheel affect the distance the bicycle travels?
support.frame: A bigger wheel travels ___ with each pedal rotation because ___ .
support.explanation: The bigger the front wheel, the longer its perimeter, so one pedal rotation carries the bicycle a greater distance. A smaller front wheel would travel a shorter distance with each pedal rotation.

support.prompt: Predict the total spaces for these settings. Give the answer in spaces. Round to four decimal places if needed.
parameters: Seats or tiles in each row: 4
support.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24. Perimeter: 20 units. Count equal rows to find the total.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A rectangular game board has 6 rows and 4 spaces per row. What is its perimeter in space-width units?
support.explanation: The sides measure 6 and 4 units, so the perimeter is 2(6 + 4) = 20 units.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: Another board has 3 rows and 8 spaces per row. How much greater is its perimeter than the 6-by-4 board?
support.explanation: The 3-by-8 board has perimeter 22. Both boards have area 24, but 22 − 20 = 2 more units of perimeter.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The table shows 1 disc → 1 step, 2 discs → 3 steps, 3 discs → 7 steps. What is the pattern rule for the number of steps when you add one more disc?
choices: Add 2 to the number of steps
Add the number of discs to the steps
Multiply the number of steps by 3
Double the number of steps and add 1
core.explanation: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3 and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7, so each new disc doubles the steps and adds 1.
feedback: Adding 2 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 + 2 = 5, and the table says 7.
Adding the discs fits 1 → 3 (1 + 2) but fails the next row: 3 + 3 = 6, and the table says 7.
Multiplying by 3 fits 1 → 3 but fails the next row: 3 × 3 = 9, and the table says 7.
hints: Test each rule on BOTH jumps: 1 → 3 and 3 → 7.
Several rules pass the first jump; only one passes both.
What do you do to 3 to land exactly on 7?

core.prompt: Use the pattern rule to complete the table: how many steps for a four-disc tower?
core.explanation: A three-disc tower takes 7 steps, so a four-disc tower takes 7 × 2 + 1 = 15 steps.
feedback: 9 adds 2 to 7 instead of doubling and adding 1.
14 doubles the 7 steps but forgets to add 1.
28 multiplies 7 by 4 (the number of discs) instead of doubling once and adding 1.
hints: Start from the three-disc answer: 7 steps.
Apply the rule: double, then add 1.

core.prompt: What is the minimum number of steps to solve a FIVE-disc Tower of Hanoi puzzle?
core.explanation: A four-disc tower takes 15 steps, so a five-disc tower takes 15 × 2 + 1 = 31 steps.
feedback: 15 steps is the answer for FOUR discs — the fifth disc requires applying the rule once more.
30 doubles the 15 steps but forgets to add 1.
35 adds 5 discs × 4 to 15 — the rule is double and add 1, not add a multiple of the discs.
hints: You need the four-disc answer first: 15.
Apply the rule one more time.

core.prompt: Why is finding a pattern MORE powerful than just solving the three-disc puzzle by hand?
choices: The pattern lets you skip the rules of the puzzle
The pattern predicts the answer for towers you have never played, like five or six discs
Patterns make the discs move by themselves
A pattern proves the puzzle is impossible
core.explanation: The pattern told us a five-disc tower needs a minimum of 31 steps — without moving a single disc.
feedback: The rules always apply — the pattern predicts the move COUNT, it does not change what moves are legal.
You still make every move yourself; the pattern only tells you how many to expect.
The pattern shows the puzzle IS solvable at every size, and says how many steps it takes.
hints: What did the table tell us about the five-disc tower?
Did we ever play the five-disc tower by hand?
Prediction is the power.

core.prompt: How can you ORGANIZE the information about discs and moves to help you see patterns?
core.frame: I can organize the information in a ___ .
core.explanation: I can create a table with one column for the number of discs and one for the number of steps: 1 and 1, 2 and 3, 3 and 7, 4 and 15, 5 and 31. With the numbers lined up in rows, I can compare each row to the next and spot the double-and-add-1 pattern.

core.prompt: The pedal gear turns 48 teeth per rotation. The largest rear gear needs 32 teeth for one full rotation. How many rotations does the rear wheel make for each pedal rotation?
core.explanation: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5, so the rear wheel makes 1.5 rotations for each pedal rotation.
feedback: That divides 32 by 48 the wrong way around — the wheel turns MORE than once, not less.
2 rotations would need a 24-tooth gear, since 48 ÷ 24 = 2.
That subtracts 48 − 32 instead of dividing 48 by 32.
hints: The chain delivers 48 teeth of motion; the gear uses 32 per rotation.
How many groups of 32 fit in 48?
Divide 48 by 32.

core.prompt: The smallest rear gear has 12 teeth. How many rotations will the rear wheel make for each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear?
core.explanation: 48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the rear wheel makes 4 rotations for each pedal rotation.
feedback: That divides 12 by 48 the wrong way around — the small gear turns MORE than the pedal gear, not less.
3 rotations would need a 16-tooth gear, since 48 ÷ 16 = 3.
That subtracts 48 − 12 instead of dividing 48 by 12.
hints: The chain delivers 48 teeth of motion; this gear uses only 12 per rotation.
How many groups of 12 fit in 48?
Divide 48 by 12.

core.prompt: You are about to ride up a steep hill. Which rear gear should the chain be on, and why?
choices: The 12-tooth gear, because 4 rotations per pedal is always better
The 32-tooth gear, because it makes the bike go faster
It does not matter which gear you use on a hill
The 32-tooth gear, because 1.5 rotations per pedal makes pedaling easier at slow speeds
core.explanation: The larger gear turns the wheel fewer times per pedal rotation, which makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds or go uphill.
feedback: The 12-tooth gear is for speed on flat ground or downhill — on a hill it makes each pedal push much harder.
The 32-tooth gear is the slower gear, not the faster one; its advantage on a hill is easier pedaling.
It matters a great deal — that is the whole point of having gears of different sizes.
hints: Uphill, you want each pedal push to be easier, not faster.
Which gear gives FEWER wheel rotations per pedal rotation?
The larger gear: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 rotations.

core.prompt: With the chain on the 12-tooth gear, the rider makes 10 pedal rotations. How many rotations does the rear wheel make?
core.explanation: The rear wheel makes 4 rotations per pedal rotation, so 10 pedal rotations give 10 × 4 = 40 wheel rotations.
feedback: That adds 10 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 10 + 12 instead of using the 4-rotations-per-pedal ratio.
That multiplies 10 by the 12 teeth instead of by the 4 rotations per pedal rotation.
hints: First find the rotations per single pedal rotation: 48 ÷ 12.
That is 4 wheel rotations for each pedal rotation.
Now scale up: 10 pedal rotations × 4.

core.prompt: Why do you think the larger gear makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds?
core.frame: With the larger gear, each pedal rotation only turns the wheel ___ .
core.explanation: With the larger gear the rear wheel only makes 1.5 rotations per pedal rotation instead of 4, so each pedal push moves the bike a shorter distance. Moving a shorter distance per push takes less force, which is easier when going slowly or uphill.

hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.

stretch.prompt: A five-disc tower takes 31 steps. Using the pattern rule, how many steps would a SIX-disc tower take?
stretch.explanation: Apply the rule to 31: double it and add 1, so 31 × 2 + 1 = 63 steps.
feedback: 32 adds 1 to 31 but forgets to double first.
36 adds 5 to 31 — the rule doubles the steps rather than adding the disc count.
62 doubles the 31 steps but forgets to add 1.
hints: The rule works from any row of the table.
Double, then add 1.

stretch.prompt: Look at the table a different way: 1 disc → 1, 2 discs → 3, 3 discs → 7, 4 discs → 15, 5 discs → 31. Which describes the relationship between the number of discs and the number of steps?
choices: The steps are the number of discs multiplied by itself
The steps are 6 times the number of discs, plus or minus 1
The steps are the two previous step counts added together
The steps are 1 less than a doubling pattern: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 each minus 1
stretch.explanation: 2 − 1 = 1, 4 − 1 = 3, 8 − 1 = 7, 16 − 1 = 15, 32 − 1 = 31 — every entry is one less than the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
feedback: Discs times itself gives 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 — that misses the table from the second row on.
6 times the discs gives 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 — even allowing plus or minus 1, that fails the first rows.
Adding previous entries gives 1 + 3 = 4 for the third row, but the table says 7.
hints: Write the doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 above the steps 1, 3, 7, 15, 31.
Compare them row by row.
How far apart is each pair?

stretch.prompt: The 15 Puzzle is a sliding puzzle with 15 tiles in a frame 4 tiles high by 4 tiles wide. You arrange the tiles from 1 to 15 by sliding one tile at a time into the open space. Sometimes it is solvable and sometimes it is not. How would you make an argument about whether a particular 15 Puzzle is solvable, using what this lesson taught about being playful?
stretch.explanation: I would play the way we played the Tower of Hanoi: start with small cases and look for patterns. The frame is 4 × 4 = 16 spaces holding 15 tiles, so there is exactly one open space to slide into. I would try to solve it, keep track of which arrangements I can reach, and look for a pattern or relationship in the tile positions that separates the solvable starting setups from the impossible ones. If every attempt at a certain arrangement fails the same way, that repeated pattern becomes my evidence for arguing it is unsolvable.

stretch.prompt: The rider makes 3 full pedal rotations with the chain on the 32-tooth gear. How many rotations does the rear wheel make?
stretch.explanation: Three pedal rotations move 3 × 48 = 144 teeth of chain, and 144 ÷ 32 = 4.5 rear-wheel rotations.
feedback: 3 rotations forgets the gear ratio — the wheel turns 1.5 times for EACH pedal rotation, not once.
6 uses a ratio of 2 rotations per pedal, but 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5, not 2.
96 is 3 × 32, which multiplies by the gear's teeth instead of finding rotations.
hints: Each pedal rotation gives 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 wheel rotations.
You have 3 pedal rotations.
Multiply 3 × 1.5.

stretch.prompt: A designer adds a middle gear so the rear wheel makes exactly 2 rotations per rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear. How many teeth must the new gear have?
stretch.explanation: The gear must use 48 ÷ 2 = 24 teeth per rotation, so a 24-tooth gear gives exactly 2 rotations.
feedback: A 16-tooth gear gives 48 ÷ 16 = 3 rotations, not 2.
48 ÷ 22 is not a whole 2 — check that 22 × 2 does not equal 48.
96 doubles 48 instead of halving it; a 96-tooth gear would rotate only half a turn per pedal rotation.
hints: You need teeth × 2 rotations = 48 teeth of chain.
So the tooth count is 48 divided by 2.

stretch.prompt: How would the distance traveled differ with a smaller front wheel on the Penny Farthing? Use the 1 to 1 pedal ratio in your answer.
stretch.frame: The ratio stays 1 to 1, but each rotation covers ___ .
stretch.explanation: The pedal-to-wheel ratio stays 1 to 1, so each pedal rotation still gives exactly one wheel rotation. But a smaller wheel has a shorter perimeter, so each rotation rolls the bike a shorter distance — the rider would have to pedal many more times to go the same distance.
